色不異空，空不異色；色即是空，空即是色.

Every reader of the Heart Sutra eventually hits this line and asks the obvious question: if form is emptiness, why is there still a cup on the table?

The usual answers go in two directions, and both are wrong in the same way. One says emptiness is another realm behind appearances — the cup is illusion, the real is the void. The other says emptiness is a mode of describing things — the cup is real, "empty" just means it will break someday. The first makes the world a mask; the second makes emptiness a footnote.

The sutra is doing something else, and the cup itself is the cleanest way to show it.

## Wall and hollow

A cup has a wall and a hollow. The wall is 有: it can be held, filled, fired, broken. The hollow is 無: it cannot be held, and without it the cup holds nothing at all.

Nobody manufactured the hollow separately. It is not inside the cup, and it is not outside it. Remove the wall and there is no hollow left to find. The two are not two things; they are two aspects of one thing, and neither survives alone.

This is the image the Daodejing uses for 有 and 無 — 三十輻共一轂，當其無，有車之用 — and it is the image the Heart Sutra uses for 色 and 空. 色 is the wall: the assembled, functional, graspable side. 空 is the hollow: the fact that the wall has no self-supporting core.

So 空 is not the absence of the cup. It is the cup's way of being a cup.

## Why "no own-nature" is the precise claim

If 空 meant "nothing," then 度一切苦厄 would collapse: there would be no suffering to cross over. The sutra would be a tranquilizer, not a teaching.

空 means 無自性: no independent, unchanging core. The five aggregates — 色, 受, 想, 行, 識 — are each assembled from conditions. While assembled they function, and function is real. Dismantled, there is no remainder you can point to and say "this was the thing itself."

Which is why the sutra can say both 色即是空 and 空即是色 without contradiction. Not two statements about two worlds, but one statement about one world seen twice.

## 三才 and 五蘊 in one vessel

The frame I work with places 天, 地, 人 and the five aggregates inside the same cup.

- 色 belongs to 地: the material side, the wall.
- 受, 想, 行, 識 belong to 人: the felt, the named, the driven, the known.
- 空 is 太極: not a fourth thing beside the three, but the fact that the vessel as a whole is assembled and has no core.

三才 gives the scale — heaven, earth and human are in one vessel, and the visible and invisible share a source. 五蘊 gives the layers — body, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness. Put together, the cup is not a metaphor for the person; it is the person's structure shown as a vessel.

And the conclusion is not "break the cup." Breaking it produces shards, not emptiness. The conclusion is: see that the cup was always assembled from conditions, and stop treating its wall as a self.

## What this does to practice

Two things change immediately.

First, emptiness stops being an experience to chase. You do not need to feel spacious, dissolved, or thought-free. You need to see the assembly — this feeling arose from these conditions, this "I" is a label on the assembly. The seeing can happen in an ordinary, unspectacular moment.

Second, 無常 stops being bad news. If things had own-nature, they could not change; change would be annihilation. Because they are empty, change is possible, and so is the end of suffering. 空 is the reason practice is possible at all, not the reason it is pointless.

## Where the book stops

36 sections, 71,207 characters of commentary, appendices A–O. Every section states its own limit: what the base text supports, what the variants leave open, and where the argument has to stop and hand the question back to the reader.

The three figures are included as inline SVG: the 般若名相總綱, the 三才五蘊太極空杯, and the 色空不二 open cup with its two grips.
